newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks fall, dollar down after U.S. slide.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks fall, dollar down after U.S. slide.

text.p: A slide in U.S. markets spilled over into Tokyo trading on Thursday, as a weaker Wall Street dragged down Japanese stocks and the dollar faltered on fears of an early rise in Japan's rock-bottom interest rates.

The key Tokyo stock market index shed more than 100 points in early trade, hurt by the overnight battering of U.S. blue-chips, but the knock-on effect proved less damaging than traders had feared before the market opened.
In mid-morning trading, the benchmark Nikkei 225 average was down 102.92 points, or 0.50 percent, at 20,465.46 -- a moderate drop. The index had fallen as low as 20,341.19 soon after the opening.

On Wednesday, U.S. stocks, the dollar and bonds all tumbled on renewed fears that U.S. interest rates would head higher, fresh worries about U.S. corporate earnings, and concern about the attractiveness of dollar-based assets.
The U.S. markets' anxiety attack was fuelled by comments by a senior Goldman Sachs official who questioned whether Japanese investors were losing their appetite for U.S. Treasuries.
But despite the U.S. markets hangover, stock brokers said the Nikkei index would find support at around 20,200 to 20,300.
"The Nikkei average is likely to test the bottom. But market players might wait and see the New York market later today," said one broker.
The dollar, meanwhile, fell against the yen and mark in thin Tokyo trading after comments from a senior central banker suggested Japan may see an early rise in interest rates.
The dollar stood at around 112.60 yen and 1.5380 marks in mid-morning trade, below its late-U.S. level of around 112.97 yen and 1.5378 marks.

A Japanese financial daily on Thursday quoted a Bank of Japan official as saying that, since Japan's economy was stronger than expected, Japan may adjust its monetary policy before seeing the effect of a planned consumption tax next April.

Traders took this as a signal that the central bank could raise its key interest rate, which has been held at a record low of 0.5 percent to bolster a fragile economic recovery, sooner than otherwise expected.
A dealer at a European bank said this prompted a slew of dollar sales as the market mood had already been darkened by the falls in U.S. financial markets overnight.
"The dollar might have found the bottom on a daily basis, but on a longer-term basis, it is likely to slide more," the dealer said.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 70.73 points, or 1.09 percent, at 6,402.52 on Wednesday.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury fell more than 1-3/4 points in U.S. trading on Wednesday, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, shot up to 6.63 percent -- its highest since early November -- against 6.49 percent on Tuesday.

The steep fall in U.S. Treasuries overnight also cast a shadow over Japanese government bond futures. In Thursday morning trade in Tokyo, the March contract was down 0.36 point at 124.88 after opening at 124.64.
"Market sentiment is weak. Dealers who bought recently are likely to unload their positions. There are also those who are creating new short positions," said a trader at a trust bank.
